title: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

sheetTitle.es: La guerra de 1812 y la doctrina Monroe, 1807–1823

summary: Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

layers.name: Historic National Boundaries: 1800
layers.shows: Borders in 1800, before the Louisiana Purchase, with the United States shaded pink. Each pop-up names the country.
layers.source: University of Minnesota (historic national boundaries), from the MapMaker catalogue

layers.name: Land Spain gave up in 1819
layers.shows: Land Spain gave up in the Adams–Onís Treaty, including East and West Florida (green). Each pop-up gives a short note.

layers.name: Battlefield Boundaries: War of 1812
layers.shows: The land each battlefield covered (tan) and its core area (lighter tan). Each pop-up gives the battle and its size in acres.
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819
layers.shows: The 1819 boundary with Spain as a pink dashed line in seven parts, drawn from the treaty's description and approximate. Each pop-up describes its part.
layers.source: Treaty text from the Avalon Project, Yale Law School; drawn on Natural Earth rivers

layers.name: Battles of the War of 1812
layers.shows: 52 battles from 1811 to 1815 as diamonds: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if inconclusive; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. Each pop-up gives the dates, the victor, total casualties, a casualties chart, the leaders on each side and a short account. The legend labels every opponent of the United States as British, but some battles were fought against Native nations: Tippecanoe (the Shawnee-led confederacy), Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend (Red Stick Creeks). The pop-up's leaders and story say who fought.
layers.source: American Battlefield Trust (War of 1812 Battles map)

layers.name: Latin American independence and US recognition
layers.shows: Ten Latin American nations, labeled with the year of independence: blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824, orange diamonds if it recognized them later (1826 to 1862). Each pop-up gives the capital, today's countries, independence and recognition.
layers.source: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State; Library of Congress country studies

knownIssues.note: The Victor field's labels are American Side Victory and British Side Victory for every battle, so Fort Mims shows as a British victory and Horseshoe Bend as a victory over the British; both were fought against Red Stick Creek forces, and Tippecanoe against the Shawnee-led confederacy. Raised with the MapMaker team: relabel as Side A / Side B or add an opponent field.

knownIssues.where: Latin American independence and US recognition
knownIssues.note: The legend groups recognition as by 1824 or later, while question 4 asks about recognition before December 2, 1823; Brazil and Central America (1824) fall in the blue group. The pop-up date settles it. A three-way grouping (before the message, after it, later) would be clearer.

compellingQuestion.en: How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo cambiaron la guerra de 1812 y los años siguientes el lugar de Estados Unidos en América del Norte y del Sur?

questions.task: Open The War of 1812 bookmark and use the battle diamonds to find the three main areas of fighting.

student.en: Open The War of 1812 bookmark and click some diamonds in each group. In which three areas was most of the fighting?
student.es: Abre el marcador The War of 1812 (La guerra de 1812) y haz clic en algunos rombos de cada grupo. ¿En qué tres zonas se combatió más?

answer.where: The War of 1812 bookmark; Battles of the War of 1812 layer. The pop-up gives the battle name and its State Name field; the legend gives the result by color. Three clusters: the Great Lakes and the border with British Canada (pop-ups say Michigan, Ohio, New York, Ontario); Chesapeake Bay (Maryland, Virginia); the Gulf Coast and Alabama (Alabama, Louisiana).
answer.accept: Three areas named by region or by the states in the pop-ups: the Canadian border and Great Lakes; the Chesapeake Bay area around Washington and Baltimore; the South along the Gulf Coast and in Alabama. Accept the Creek War battles in Alabama as part of the southern area.
answer.text: Around Chesapeake Bay the British won at Bladensburg and burned Washington, then failed to take Baltimore. The Alabama battles were the Creek War against the Red Stick Creeks. The layer also includes Tippecanoe (November 1811), fought before the war against a Native confederacy; a battle diamond may sit on tan battlefield land, so the pop-up may say 1 of 2.

questions.task: Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.

student.en: Click the three biggest diamonds. Where and when was each battle fought, and who won? The peace treaty was signed at Ghent, in Europe, on December 24, 1814. Which big battle came after it?
student.es: Haz clic en los tres rombos más grandes. ¿Dónde y cuándo se libró cada batalla, y quién ganó? El tratado de paz se firmó en Gante, en Europa, el 24 de diciembre de 1814. ¿Qué gran batalla fue posterior al tratado?

answer.where: Battles of the War of 1812 layer, the three largest diamonds: pop-up fields Battle Dates, Battle Victor and Total Casualties, with the state in State Name. Legend: blue = American victory, red = British victory, gray = inconclusive. The table lists the five largest in case students pick a different third.

table.caption: Battles with the most casualties, from the pop-ups
rows: American victory over the Red Stick Creeks

answer.accept: The three battles with the most casualties, each with place, date and result from the pop-up; New Orleans (January 8, 1815) identified as the battle fought after the Treaty of Ghent.
answer.text: Fort Erie, New Orleans and Lundy's Lane are the three largest; news of the peace hadn't crossed the Atlantic before New Orleans. Horseshoe Bend (fourth largest) was fought against the Red Stick Creeks, not the British: the legend's British label is the layer's simplification, and the pop-up names Menawa as the opposing leader.

questions.task: Open The 1819 boundary bookmark, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and read their pop-ups to describe what the treaty settled.

student.en: Open The 1819 boundary bookmark. Turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819, and click the green land and each part of the pink dashed line. What did the United States gain from Spain? Which rivers and lines of latitude and longitude does the new border follow?
student.es: Abre el marcador The 1819 boundary (La frontera de 1819). En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa las capas Land Spain gave up in 1819 (tierra que España cedió en 1819) y Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 (línea del tratado Adams-Onís, 1819). Haz clic en la tierra verde y en cada tramo de la línea discontinua rosada. ¿Qué obtuvo Estados Unidos de España? ¿Qué ríos y qué líneas de latitud y longitud sigue la nueva frontera?

answer.where: The 1819 boundary bookmark. Land Spain gave up in 1819 layer: green areas East Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819, West Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819 and Spanish Cession 1819; the Notes in each pop-up say the land came through the Adams-Onís Treaty and the United States assumed $5 million in claims instead of paying. Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 layer, pop-ups part 1 to part 7: the Sabine River north to 32° N; north to the Red River; the Red River west to 100° W; north along 100° W to the Arkansas River; the Arkansas upstream to its source; north to 42° N; west along 42° N to the Pacific.
answer.accept: Florida (East and West) gained from Spain, with the $5 million in claims if read; the border described using at least the Sabine, Red and Arkansas rivers, 100° W and 42° N, in order from the Gulf to the Pacific.
answer.text: The United States already held much of West Florida. The treaty was signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821. The line is drawn from the treaty's description and is approximate, as each pop-up's note says.

title.en: New nations and the Monroe Doctrine
title.es: Nuevas naciones y la doctrina Monroe

questions.task: Open Latin America in 1825, turn on the independence layer, and compare the dates of independence and US recognition with President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.

student.en: Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark and turn on Latin American independence and US recognition. Click the blue circles and read each recognition date in the pop-up: which nations had the United States recognized before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823? (Blue means recognized by 1824, so check the date.) Why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out of the Americas?
student.es: Abre el marcador Latin America in 1825 (América Latina en 1825) y activa la capa Latin American independence and US recognition (independencia latinoamericana y reconocimiento de Estados Unidos). Haz clic en los círculos azules y lee la fecha de reconocimiento en cada ventana emergente: ¿qué naciones había reconocido Estados Unidos antes del mensaje del presidente Monroe del 2 de diciembre de 1823? (El azul significa reconocida en 1824 o antes, así que comprueba la fecha.) ¿Por qué crees que Monroe advirtió a las potencias europeas que no intervinieran en América?

answer.where: Latin America in 1825 bookmark; Latin American independence and US recognition layer (legend: blue circle = recognized by the United States by 1824, orange diamond = recognized later). Six blue circles; the pop-up's US recognition line gives the date. Before December 2, 1823: Republic of Colombia (June 19, 1822), Mexico (December 12, 1822), Buenos Ayres (January 27, 1823) and Chile (January 27, 1823). Brazil (May 26, 1824) and the Federation of Central America (August 4, 1824) are blue but were recognized after the message.

table.caption: Recognized by the United States by 1824, from the pop-ups

answer.accept: The four nations recognized before the message, read from the pop-up dates (not all six blue circles); a reason for the warning that uses the map, such as new independent nations across the Americas that European powers might try to take back, or the United States wanting to be the main power in the region.
answer.text: Monroe warned European powers not to set up new colonies in the Americas or interfere with the newly independent nations, and said the United States would stay out of Europe's wars. Haiti, independent since 1804, was not recognized until 1862 (orange diamond).

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch of the three war fronts and of the 1819 border and the area the Monroe Doctrine covered (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. Accept answers that use the battles to show the war ended without gains, the 1819 layers to show the United States growing and fixing its border with Spain, and the independence layer to show the new nations the Monroe Doctrine spoke for.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

objectives: Use the battle diamonds in the Battles of the War of 1812 layer to identify the three main areas of fighting.
Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.
Read the pop-ups of the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line layers to describe what the treaty settled.
Compare the dates of independence and US recognition in the Latin American independence layer with Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
Use the locations of the battles and the 1819 boundary as evidence to explain how the United States' position in North America changed between 1812 and 1823.
discussion: The battle diamonds cluster in three areas far apart. From the map, what was each side trying to control in each area, and why was none of them decisive?
The Battle of New Orleans was fought after the Treaty of Ghent was signed. Looking at where Ghent and New Orleans are, what does that gap tell you about how news travelled and how wars ended in 1815?

Most Latin American nations had declared independence before Monroe's 1823 message, and the United States recognized several of them. Comparing the dates on the map, was the Monroe Doctrine leading events or following them?

beforeYouStart.en: In the early 1800s Britain and France were at war, and both seized American ships. British warships also forced sailors off American ships into the Royal Navy, and Britain supported Native nations resisting American settlement. In June 1812 the United States declared war on Britain.
beforeYouStart.es: A comienzos del siglo XIX, Gran Bretaña y Francia estaban en guerra, y ambas se apoderaban de barcos estadounidenses. Además, los buques de guerra británicos obligaban a marineros de barcos estadounidenses a servir en la Marina Real, y Gran Bretaña apoyaba a los pueblos indígenas que se resistían a los asentamientos estadounidenses. En junio de 1812, Estados Unidos le declaró la guerra a Gran Bretaña.

readingTheMap.en: The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows the United States in 1800. Diamonds mark battles; use the legend: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if neither side won; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. The legend says British for every opponent, but some battles were fought against Native nations: the pop-up's leaders and story tell you who fought. Each battle pop-up gives the dates, the victor and the casualties. Tan shading shows battlefield land. Three layers are off when the map opens: the land Spain gave up in 1819 (green), the treaty line (pink dashes, in seven parts) and the Latin American nations, shown as blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824 and orange diamonds if later; the pop-up gives the exact date.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares: haz clic en un elemento para ver su nombre. El sombreado rosado muestra Estados Unidos en 1800. Los rombos marcan las batallas; usa la leyenda: azul si ganaron los estadounidenses, rojo si ganaron los británicos y gris si ningún bando ganó; los rombos más grandes indican más bajas. La leyenda dice británicos para todos los adversarios, pero algunas batallas se libraron contra naciones indígenas: los líderes y el relato de la ventana emergente dicen quién combatió. La ventana emergente de cada batalla da las fechas, el vencedor y las bajas. El sombreado color canela muestra el terreno de los campos de batalla. Tres capas están desactivadas al abrir el mapa: la tierra que España cedió en 1819 (verde), la línea del tratado (rayas rosadas, en siete tramos) y las naciones latinoamericanas, que aparecen como círculos azules si Estados Unidos las reconoció en 1824 o antes y como rombos naranjas si fue más tarde; la ventana emergente da la fecha exacta.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about the War of 1812 and its results that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre la guerra de 1812 y sus resultados que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: When the map opens, the boundaries and battles are on and three layers are off: Land Spain gave up in 1819, Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819, and Latin American independence and US recognition. Students turn them on for questions 3 and 4.

misconceptions.claim: The United States won the War of 1812 and gained land.
misconceptions.response: The Treaty of Ghent returned the borders to where they were before the war, and the map shows American and British victories on every front.

misconceptions.claim: The Battle of New Orleans won the war.
misconceptions.response: It was fought on January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814.

misconceptions.claim: Every battle was against British soldiers.
misconceptions.response: The battles in Alabama were part of the Creek War, fought against the Red Stick Creeks.

misconceptions.claim: Every blue circle was recognized before the Monroe Doctrine.
misconceptions.response: Blue means recognized by the end of 1824. Brazil and the Federation of Central America were recognized in 1824, after Monroe's message of December 2, 1823; the pop-up dates show it.

standards.text: Explain the causes, important events, and effects of the War of 1812
Identify the foreign policies of presidents Washington through Monroe and explain the impact of Washington's Farewell Address and the Monroe Doctrine

Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness (War of 1812, Convention of 1818, Adams-Onis Treaty, Missouri Compromise, Monroe Doctrine, Trail of Tears, Texas annexation, Manifest Destiny, Oregon Territory, Mexican American War/Mexican Cession, California Gold Rush, Compromise of 1850, Kansas Nebraska Act, Gadsden Purchase).
Analyze connections among events and developments in broader historical contexts.
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
